While Apple has long positioned privacy as a selling point for its hardware and services, I can't help but wonder if Apple now regrets introducing a privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

A seemingly narrow feature has faced a new antitrust lawsuit or regulatory challenge nearly every month or two. This month, a third lawsuit targeting ATT has emerged in the UK — and this one is a little different.

This article has been updated and includes Apple's response at the end...

The Personalised Advertising Controversy

Personalised advertising has long been one of the most contentious issues in tech. The ads we see are no longer random, scattershot suggestions, but rather tailored to our interests — gathered through the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win-win for everyone. Consumers see ads they may genuinely be interested in; advertisers get better returns from precise targeting; and free apps and websites that rely on ad revenue likewise benefit from the higher revenue this generates.

Although the data used to serve personalised ads is collected anonymously, the practice is widely perceived as an invasion of privacy. Even though Apple deliberately developed a technology to ensure data anonymity, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency was designed to address these concerns by giving consumers a choice over whether their data can be used to serve personalised ads. Developers must obtain consumer consent before collecting such data.

However, for the iPhone maker, this move has triggered a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, most of which centre on one fact: Apple's own apps do not need to seek this consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules are in fact consistent — Apple's own apps do not display the ATT prompt because they do not collect such data in the first place. Likewise, third-party apps that do not collect this type of data are also exempt and need not display the prompt.

The Latest UK Lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three claims before the UK's relevant antitrust regulator, the Competition Appeal Tribunal. Apple lost the first case and is currently appealing; the second is still ongoing.

Reuters reported on the latest lawsuit filed today.

What's Different

What makes this latest lawsuit particularly intriguing is that the plaintiff, Ann Pope, was once a senior official at the very regulator handling the case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, is the representative plaintiff in this lawsuit. She stated that Apple's policies "have caused very significant harm to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." Pope noted in a statement: "This lawsuit is vital to protecting the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, ensuring that the rules Apple sets are fair and just, and providing compensation for the losses suffered by UK businesses."

Apple previously agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU following an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator. Regarding this lawsuit, Apple told us:

Over the years, many privacy advocates have publicly voiced their support for ATT.
